newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sorghum plantings seen at 11 to 12 mln acres.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sorghum plantings seen at 11 to 12 mln acres.

text.p: Early projections suggest U.S. growers will plant 11 million to 12 million acres of sorghum this spring, down from 13.3 million in 1996 but still above the historical average, grain analysts said Monday.

Sources said actual sorghum acreage will depend on how much traditional cotton and wheat acreage stays devoted to sorghum. Many acres were shifted out of those crops in 1996 because of the parching effects of a severe drought.
In its baseline projection released Feb 24, the U.S. Department of Agriculture pegged U.S. sorghum plantings at 11.3 million acres.

But Sid Love, analyst with Kropf-Love Consulting, said he expected at least 11.5 million acres to be planted to sorghum. Love said sorghum plantings may be greater than 11.5 million acres depending on how much traditional hard red winter wheat acreage stays devoted to sorghum--also called milo.
"We planted almost two million acres less hard red winter wheat last fall than people expected, so I think the final sorghum estimate will be higher (than USDA's baseline projection)," Love said.
Kansas farmers planted 4.8 million acres to sorghum in 1996, up from 3.3 million in 1995.

The high level of acreage, coupled with timely, drought-busting summer rains, allowed Kansas producers to harvest a record 354.2 million bushels in 1996 -- well above the previous high of 311.25 million bushels in 1986.
Tim Lust, director of marketing for National Grain Sorghum Producers, estimated 1997 U.S. sorghum plantings at 12 million acres, plus or minus 500,000 acres.

As was the case with wheat producers in Kansas, many cotton producers in Texas shifted to sorghum in 1996 because of the drought. Texas growers planted 4.4 million acres of sorghum in 1996, well above the 2.7 million in 1995.
Lust said that although Kansas acreage will probably stay at the same level as last year, some Texas producers will likely switch back to cotton.
"I feel like we will lose some acres in southern Texas, Panhandle and south Plains areas unless we have weather problems late in the season," Lust said.

Sources said sorghum seed remains in high demand across the central Plains, which could signal robust plantings. Nathan Boardman, president of Crosbyton Seeds, a Texas seed research, development, production and packaging firm, said the industry was currently experiencing a shortage of seed.
"I believe there will be enough sorghum seed to plant, but if a (grower) is just sold on one particular variety he might have to take a substitute variety."
Boardman said he anticipated at least 11 million acres would be planted to sorghum.
All analysts cautioned that their numbers were just projections, and they said they would be waiting to see the official USDA Prospective Plantings report, due out March 31.

Barb Kliment, a spokeswoman for the Nebraska Grain Sorghum Board, said a lot could change between now and planting season. She also noted that any projections were complicated by Freedom to Farm -- the new U.S. agriculture policy that gives farmers more flexibility in choosing what to plant.

"It's probably early yet for growers to be making real decisions over what to plant, and of course Freedom to Farm quite frankly holds a whole new set of conditions for growers in terms of decision-making," Kliment said.
